subject: environmental-systems
title: Environmental Systems MYP 5 Full eAssessment Mock

questions.content:
A research team studied energy flow in a grassland ecosystem. The energy stored in each trophic level in one year is shown in kJ per m² per year.

Grass (producers): 15 000
Rabbits (primary consumers): 1 500
Foxes (secondary consumers): 120

(a) State what the arrows in a food web represent. (1 mark)
(b) Name the organism at the second trophic level. (1 mark)
(c) Calculate the percentage of energy transferred from the grass to the rabbits and from the rabbits to the foxes. (2 marks)
(d) Explain why only a small proportion of energy is passed on at each trophic level. (2 marks)
(e) Explain why food chains rarely have more than five trophic levels. (2 marks)
(f) A disease kills most of the rabbits. Predict the effect on the fox population and on the grass, and justify each prediction. (3 marks)

(Total 11 marks)
questions.mark_scheme:
(a) [1] The direction of energy (and matter) flow, from the organism eaten to the organism that eats it
(b) [1] Rabbits (primary consumers)
(c) [1] 1 500 ÷ 15 000 × 100 = 10%
[1] 120 ÷ 1 500 × 100 = 8%
(d) [1] Energy is lost as heat from respiration and in movement and life processes
[1] Energy is lost in uneaten parts, faeces and waste, which pass to decomposers
(e) [1] At each step only about 10% (or a small fraction) of energy is passed on, so very little remains at the top
[1] There is not enough energy to support a viable population of a further consumer
(f) [1] Foxes decline (or switch to other prey) because their food supply falls
[1] Grass increases because there is less grazing
[1] Justification linked to food-web relationships (foxes depend on rabbits; rabbits eat grass), accept a mention that the changes may be limited if foxes have other prey
Common error: saying the energy 'disappears'.

questions.content:
Warm water is released by a power station into a river. A team measured the dissolved oxygen concentration in water samples held at different temperatures in the laboratory.

Temperature (°C): 10, 15, 20, 25, 30
Dissolved oxygen (mg per dm³): 11.3, 10.1, 9.1, 8.3, 7.5

(a) Describe the pattern in the data. (1 mark)
(b) Calculate the average change in dissolved oxygen per °C between 10 °C and 30 °C. (2 marks)
(c) Explain the effects of this change on fish living near the outflow of the power station. (3 marks)
(d) The team will now investigate the hypothesis: "The number of invertebrate species is lower close to the power station outflow than 500 m upstream." Design a fieldwork method to test this hypothesis. Your answer should include the variables, the method, how you would make the data reliable and one safety precaution. (6 marks)

(Total 12 marks)
questions.mark_scheme:
(a) [1] As temperature rises, dissolved oxygen concentration falls (negative relationship)
(b) [1] (7.5 − 11.3) ÷ 20
[1] −0.19 mg per dm³ per °C (a decrease of 0.19)
(c) [1] Warm water holds less dissolved oxygen, and fish need oxygen for respiration
[1] Fish gills cannot obtain enough oxygen, so fish become stressed or less active, and growth and breeding fall
[1] Some species leave or die, so biodiversity near the outflow falls (accept: warmer water also increases fish metabolic rate so demand rises)
(d) [1] Independent variable: location (near the outflow compared with upstream); dependent variable: number of invertebrate species
[1] Method: kick-sampling or netting for the same fixed time (for example 3 minutes) at each site
[1] Controlled variables: same net, same time, same depth and flow speed, same time of day, same person
[1] Reliability: repeat the sample at least three times at each site and calculate a mean
[1] Identification of organisms using a key, and recording results in a table
[1] A safety precaution such as wearing waders or a life jacket, working in pairs, avoiding fast water, or washing hands afterwards
Common error: failing to state how the variable would be measured.

questions.content:
A weather station on an island recorded the mean annual air temperature in four different years.

Year: 1990, 2000, 2010, 2020
Mean temperature (°C): 9.1, 9.4, 9.8, 10.3

(a) Calculate the mean change in temperature per decade between 1990 and 2020. (2 marks)
(b) Assuming the rate stays the same, predict the mean temperature in 2040. (1 mark)
(c) Evaluate the reliability of this prediction. (2 marks)
(d) Describe how you would present these data in a graph. (2 marks)
(e) Explain how burning fossil fuels contributes to global warming. (3 marks)
(f) Distinguish between weather and climate. (2 marks)

(Total 12 marks)
questions.mark_scheme:
(a) [1] (10.3 − 9.1) ÷ 3 decades
[1] 0.4 °C per decade
(b) [1] 10.3 + 2 × 0.4 = 11.1 °C
(c) [1] Only four data points over a short period, and the rate may not stay constant (it could accelerate or slow with emissions or policy)
[1] Natural variation and other factors are ignored; the prediction is a rough estimate and should be shown with a range
(d) [1] A line graph with year on the x-axis and mean temperature on the y-axis
[1] Labelled axes with units, a suitable scale, plotted points joined or with a line of best fit and a title
(e) [1] Burning fossil fuels releases CO₂ into the atmosphere
[1] CO₂ is a greenhouse gas that absorbs infrared radiation emitted by Earth's surface
[1] This traps more heat (the enhanced greenhouse effect), so average temperatures increase
(f) [1] Weather is the short-term state of the atmosphere in a place (for example today's rain or temperature)
[1] Climate is the average of weather over a long period, usually 30 years or more
Common error: describing weather as 'local' and climate as 'global' only.

questions.content:
A remote village uses 600 MWh of electricity each year. It currently uses a diesel generator and is considering a solar farm instead.

Diesel generator: emits 0.80 tonnes of CO₂ per MWh; running cost $240 per MWh.
Solar farm: emits 0.04 tonnes of CO₂ per MWh (from manufacturing and maintenance); running cost $15 per MWh; capital cost $1 200 000 per MW of capacity. The solar farm produces on average 18% of its capacity (capacity factor 0.18). There are 8 760 hours in a year.

(a) Calculate the yearly CO₂ emissions from the diesel generator. (1 mark)
(b) Calculate the percentage reduction in yearly CO₂ emissions if the village changes to solar. (2 marks)
(c) Calculate the capacity of solar farm needed, in MW, to supply 600 MWh a year. Give your answer to 2 decimal places. (2 marks)
(d) The capital cost is $456 624 for this capacity. Calculate the annual running-cost saving and the payback time in years, to 1 decimal place. (3 marks)
(e) Explain two limitations of relying only on solar energy for the village. (2 marks)
(f) Evaluate which option the village should choose, considering environmental, economic and social factors. (4 marks)

(Total 14 marks)
questions.mark_scheme:
(a) [1] 600 × 0.80 = 480 tonnes
(b) [1] Solar emissions = 600 × 0.04 = 24 tonnes
[1] (480 − 24) ÷ 480 × 100 = 95%
(c) [1] Energy per MW = 0.18 × 8 760 = 1 576.8 MWh per MW per year (or 600 ÷ 1 576.8)
[1] 0.38 MW
(d) [1] Annual saving = (240 − 15) × 600 = $135 000
[1] Payback = 456 624 ÷ 135 000
[1] 3.4 years
(e) [1] Solar output is intermittent (no power at night or in cloudy weather), so storage or backup is needed
[1] Large land area required, high battery cost, or panels need maintenance and disposal (accept any valid limitation, explained)
(f) [1] Environmental: solar greatly reduces CO₂ (95% fewer emissions) and avoids diesel spills and air pollution
[1] Economic: high initial cost but payback in about 3.4 years and lower running costs afterwards
[1] Social: reliability, noise reduction, health benefits, local jobs and access to power for the community
[1] A clear justified judgement, for example choose solar with battery storage or keep the generator as backup
Common error: ignoring the capacity factor and assuming panels work at full power all year.

questions.content:
Eutrophication is a major problem in lakes surrounded by farmland.

(a) Define eutrophication. (2 marks)
(b) Explain how the use of fertiliser on farmland can lead to fish deaths in a nearby lake. (4 marks)
(c) A farm of 80 hectares applies 150 kg of nitrogen fertiliser per hectare. Heavy rain washes 20% of the fertiliser into the lake. Calculate the mass of nitrogen entering the lake. (2 marks)
(d) Suggest two ways farmers can reduce nutrient runoff. (2 marks)
(e) Explain how a strip of vegetation between a field and a stream reduces pollution. (2 marks)

(Total 12 marks)
questions.mark_scheme:
(a) [1] An increase in nutrients (nitrates and phosphates) in a body of water
[1] That leads to excessive growth of algae and plants and a fall in oxygen
(b) [1] Fertiliser dissolves in rainwater and runs off (leaches) into the lake
[1] The extra nutrients cause an algal bloom that blocks sunlight
[1] Plants and algae die and are decomposed by bacteria
[1] Bacteria use up the dissolved oxygen, so fish suffocate
(c) [1] 80 × 150 = 12 000 kg applied
[1] 20% of 12 000 = 2 400 kg
(d) [1] Apply the correct amount at the right time (not before heavy rain)
[1] Any one from: use manure or crop rotation, plant buffer strips, avoid steep slopes, use slow-release fertiliser
(e) [1] Plant roots absorb nutrients from runoff
[1] The vegetation slows water flow so soil particles settle, and it increases infiltration
Common error: stating that fertiliser makes the water 'hot' or toxic instead of reducing oxygen.

questions.content:
Students sampled plants along a 40 m transect from the sea edge of a sand dune to the back of the dune. At each station they measured soil moisture and counted the number of plant species in a 1 m² quadrat.

Distance from the sea (m): 0, 10, 20, 30, 40
Soil moisture (%): 2, 4, 7, 11, 15
Number of plant species: 1, 3, 4, 6, 8

(a) Describe how the students should present these data to show a possible relationship between soil moisture and species number. (2 marks)
(b) Describe the relationship shown. (2 marks)
(c) Calculate the mean number of species per quadrat. (1 mark)
(d) Explain the pattern in species number as the distance from the sea increases. (2 marks)
(e) Evaluate the reliability of the data and suggest two improvements. (3 marks)

(Total 10 marks)
questions.mark_scheme:
(a) [1] A scatter graph with soil moisture on the x-axis and number of species on the y-axis
[1] With labelled axes and units, even scales and a line of best fit
(b) [1] As soil moisture increases, the number of plant species increases (positive correlation)
[1] Quote data: for example 8 species at 15% moisture compared with 1 species at 2%
(c) [1] (1 + 3 + 4 + 6 + 8) ÷ 5 = 4.4 species
(d) [1] Near the sea there is salt spray, wind, shifting sand and little water, so only specialised plants survive
[1] Further back the soil is more stable and holds more moisture and humus, so more species can survive
(e) [1] Only one quadrat per station and one transect, so the results may not be representative
[1] Improvement: repeat with several transects and more quadrats per station and calculate means
[1] Improvement: measure other factors (for example wind, salinity) or take moisture readings at the same time on the same day
Common error: stating that moisture 'causes' species number without recognising other factors.

questions.content:
A farmer wants to know which soil holds the most water. A student tested three soils. She put 100 g of dry soil in a funnel lined with filter paper above a measuring cylinder. She poured 100 cm³ of water onto the soil and measured the volume of water that drained out after 5 minutes.

Soil type: sand, loam, clay
Volume of water drained (cm³): 82, 55, 30

(a) Write a testable hypothesis for this investigation, with a scientific reason. (2 marks)
(b) Identify the independent variable and the dependent variable. (2 marks)
(c) Calculate the volume of water retained by each soil. (2 marks)
(d) Write a conclusion that explains the results using particle size. (2 marks)
(e) Suggest two sources of error and an improvement for each. (2 marks)
(f) Evaluate which soil would be most suitable for growing crops, using the data. (2 marks)

(Total 12 marks)
questions.mark_scheme:
(a) [1] A testable prediction, for example: "Soil with smaller particles will retain more water"
[1] A scientific reason, for example: smaller particles have smaller pore spaces and larger surface area so water is held by capillary action
(b) [1] Independent variable: type of soil
[1] Dependent variable: volume of water that drained out (or was retained) after 5 minutes
(c) [1] Sand 100 − 82 = 18 cm³ and loam 100 − 55 = 45 cm³
[1] Clay 100 − 30 = 70 cm³
(d) [1] Clay retained the most water (70 cm³) and sand the least (18 cm³)
[1] Clay has very small particles with tiny pore spaces and a large surface area that hold water; sand has large particles and large gaps so water drains quickly
(e) [1] Any two sources of error such as soil packed differently, water poured at different rates, water still dripping at 5 minutes, soil not equally dry
[1] A matching improvement for each, such as packing to the same depth, pouring with a measuring cylinder at a steady rate, or timing from a fixed point
(f) [1] Loam is likely most suitable as it retains a moderate amount of water (45 cm³) while still draining enough to allow air in the soil
[1] Sand would dry out too quickly and clay could become waterlogged (data support), so a balanced soil is best
Common error: saying clay is 'best' because it holds the most water, ignoring waterlogging and aeration.

questions.content:
A tropical region has a forest area of 84 000 km² in 2005 and 71 400 km² in 2015. Forest is being cleared mainly for palm oil plantations.

(a) Calculate the area of forest lost between 2005 and 2015 and express it as a percentage of the 2005 area. (2 marks)
(b) Assuming the same area of forest is lost every decade, predict the forest area in 2025. (2 marks)
(c) A second model assumes the forest area falls by the same percentage each decade. Calculate the forest area predicted for 2025. (2 marks)
(d) Calculate the percentage difference between the predictions of the two models, relative to the second model, to 1 decimal place. (1 mark)
(e) Explain three ecological consequences of deforestation. (3 marks)
(f) Evaluate the use of palm oil plantations for local communities and recommend one way of making palm oil production more sustainable. (4 marks)

(Total 14 marks)
questions.mark_scheme:
(a) [1] 84 000 − 71 400 = 12 600 km²
[1] 12 600 ÷ 84 000 × 100 = 15%
(b) [1] Constant loss of 12 600 km² per decade
[1] 71 400 − 12 600 = 58 800 km²
(c) [1] 71 400 × 0.85 (the forest area falls to 85% each decade)
[1] 60 690 km²
(d) [1] (60 690 − 58 800) ÷ 60 690 × 100 = 3.1%
(e) [1] Loss of habitat reduces biodiversity and may cause extinctions
[1] Soil erosion and loss of fertility, because there are no roots or leaf cover to protect soil
[1] Carbon released as trees are cleared and burned, and less CO₂ absorbed by photosynthesis; accept changes to rainfall and water cycle (any three consequences with explanations, one mark each)
(f) [1] Benefits: jobs, income and infrastructure for local communities
[1] Costs: loss of forest resources, food and cultural land, and pollution of water
[1] A clear evaluative judgement that weighs the short-term gains against the long-term costs
[1] A realistic sustainable approach, for example certified sustainable palm oil, planting on already degraded land, wildlife corridors or smallholder training
Common error: giving the percentage loss relative to 2015 instead of 2005.

questions.content:
A rare species of sea turtle nests on a protected beach. Conservationists collect eggs, hatch them in safe hatcheries and release the young. The number of nesting females recorded was 40 in 2005 and 112 in 2025.

(a) Define biodiversity. (1 mark)
(b) Describe three threats to biodiversity in coastal ecosystems. (3 marks)
(c) Calculate the percentage increase in the number of nesting females between 2005 and 2025. (2 marks)
(d) Explain how protected areas and captive breeding can help conserve endangered species. (3 marks)
(e) Explain why a small population of an endangered species is at risk even if it is protected. (2 marks)

(Total 11 marks)
questions.mark_scheme:
(a) [1] The variety of living things in an area, including the number of species and the genetic variety within each species (accept: variety of ecosystems)
(b) [1] Habitat loss through coastal development or tourism
[1] Pollution such as plastic, oil or chemical runoff, or over-harvesting and fishing bycatch
[1] Climate change effects such as rising temperatures or sea level rise (or invasive species) (any three distinct threats, one mark each)
(c) [1] (112 − 40) ÷ 40 × 100
[1] 180%
(d) [1] Protected areas conserve habitat and limit human disturbance such as hunting or building
[1] Captive breeding increases the number of individuals by protecting eggs and young from predators
[1] Released animals can rebuild wild populations; justification that both methods support one another
(e) [1] Small populations have low genetic diversity, which increases inbreeding and disease vulnerability
[1] They are vulnerable to chance events such as storms or disease which could wipe out the population
Common error: saying a 180% increase means the population is now safe.
